title: Alpine Carabiner Fracture Incident - Valtournenche
premise: Three hikers in the Swiss Alps required rescue after the locking carabiners on their harnesses snapped under load while they were rappelling down a granite cliff face.

side_A.role: an advocate at a consumer-safety group
side_A.goal: pushing for a recall of the product

side_B.goal: showing the product is safe when used as directed

documents:
=== DOCUMENT 1: Incident Log - Civil Protection Alpine Rescue Unit ===

**Date:** 14 October 2023
**Location:** Valtournenche Valley, Italy
**Incident ID:** CP-2023-1014-ALP
**Status:** Closed (Rescue Completed 16 October 2023)

**1. Initial Contact and Timeline**
At 14:32 local time, the Civil Protection dispatch center received an emergency call reporting a failure of climbing hardware during a descent operation. The callers identified themselves as members of the "Alpine Safety Watch," a consumer advocacy group conducting a scheduled training session. The location was specified as the granite cliff face sector known as the West Wall, which features a vertical drop of 450 meters.

Three individuals were reported to be stranded on the rock face following the fracture of their primary anchor carabiners. The group stated they were rappelling using a 10.8 mm diameter nylon rope, a standard specification for this type of descent. The on-site medic, present as part of the training staff, assessed the three injured hikers immediately after the incident. The medic’s initial field notes indicate that all three sustained minor abrasions and exhibited signs of shock, with no broken bones detected.

**2. Rescue Operation**
A rescue helicopter was dispatched immediately upon receipt of the initial call. The aircraft arrived at the scene at 15:15 local time. The rescue crew established a contact point with the stranded hikers.

At 16:00 local time, severe weather conditions set in, including high winds and reduced visibility, which made helicopter operations unsafe. The rescue operation was suspended and could not be completed until the following day. Due to these weather delays, the rescue operation required a total of two days to fully extract the hikers from the cliff face. The hikers were secured on the rock face using secondary anchor points established by the rescue team until weather conditions improved.

**3. Equipment and Context**
The hikers involved were members of the "Alpine Safety Watch." Their harnesses had been purchased from a certified outdoor retailer in Zurich on 10 June 2023. The failed hardware involved was identified as model "SecureLock X1" carabiners, manufactured by "PeakGear Industries."

Post-incident analysis of the recovered hardware revealed that the carabiners had been subjected to a static load of 32 kN at the moment of failure. The carabiners used in the incident were within their 10-year warranty period.

**4. Post-Incident Communications**
PeakGear Industries maintains a dedicated customer support line that responded to the incident within 4 hours. The company issued a preliminary statement noting that the SecureLock X1 is compliant with EN 362 standard for climbing equipment and that the product underwent 10,000 cycle fatigue testing before release. PeakGear Industries also stated that the SecureLock X1 has a rated load capacity of 25 kN.

The Civil Protection unit has no opinion on the cause of the fracture and has referred the technical analysis to the relevant materials engineering authorities.

=== DOCUMENT 2: Witness Statement - Dr. Elena Rossi, Materials Engineer (Consumer Safety Watch) ===

**Statement Date:** 16 October 2023
**Subject:** Technical Analysis of SecureLock X1 Failure

I am a materials engineer and have been the technical lead for the Alpine Safety Watch for the past three years. I was present at the scene of the incident on 14 October 2023 and conducted the initial visual inspection of the fractured carabiner immediately after the rescue team secured the area.

The SecureLock X1 is not a reliable piece of equipment. PeakGear Industries has a history of cutting corners, and this incident is the culmination of that negligence. We have documented 12 previous reports of carabiner failures with PeakGear products in the last five years, yet they continue to sell this hardware without adequate oversight. Our group advocates for mandatory third-party certification for all climbing hardware sold in the EU precisely because of these recurring safety gaps.

Upon close examination of the fractured gate, I observed a visible crack of 2.5 mm length prior to full separation. This is not a result of user error. The fracture was caused by metal fatigue due to a microscopic manufacturing defect in the gate hinge. The material had been weakened internally long before the load was applied.

I want to be clear about the condition of the gear prior to the incident. The carabiners were inspected and found to be in pristine condition with no signs of wear or damage before the incident. There was no pitting, no corrosion, and no evidence of misuse. The claim that the user mishandled the equipment is baseless.

Furthermore, the load distribution was correct. The load was evenly distributed across the carabiner spine, as per standard safety protocols. The 32 kN load recorded in the post-incident analysis was a static load resulting from the weight of the three hikers and the tension of the rope, but the geometry of the anchor was standard. The failure was inherent to the product, not the technique.

PeakGear Industries states that their SecureLock X1 underwent 10,000 cycle fatigue testing before release. If this were true, a microscopic defect of this nature would have been identified and the batch recalled. Instead, they are pointing fingers at the users. This is a dangerous deflection. The fact that 0.5% of SecureLock X1 units returned for inspection in 2022 failed due to manufacturing defects is a known statistic that PeakGear has kept quiet about, but which corroborates our findings. The fracture was a manufacturing failure, plain and simple.

=== DOCUMENT 3: Witness Statement - Marcus Thorne, Head of Communications (PeakGear Industries) ===

**Statement Date:** 16 October 2023
**Subject:** Response to Incident Report and Technical Clarifications

On behalf of PeakGear Industries, I am responding to the recent incident in the Valtournenche Valley involving the SecureLock X1 carabiner. We take the safety of our customers seriously, and our dedicated customer support line responded to the incident within 4 hours to assist the Alpine Safety Watch team with their immediate needs.

We must correct several inaccuracies in the preliminary reports. The SecureLock X1 is a premium product that is fully compliant with the EN 362 standard for climbing equipment. It has a rated load capacity of 25 kN and underwent rigorous 10,000 cycle fatigue testing before release. The product is designed for specific usage parameters, and it is the responsibility of the user to adhere to these parameters.

Regarding the cause of the fracture, the evidence points clearly to user error. The fracture was caused by the user applying an excessive lateral force to the gate, which is outside the intended usage parameters. The post-incident analysis showed a static load of 32 kN, which exceeds the rated capacity of the carabiner. However, the critical factor was the angle of application.

We have reviewed the available data, including video evidence from the training session. Video evidence suggests the rope was inadvertently pinched between the gate and the spine, creating a shear force that exceeded the rated load. This is a common mistake among inexperienced users or those who do not follow proper technique. The rope was not positioned correctly according to standard rappelling techniques; there was contact with the carabiner gate that compromised the structural integrity.

Furthermore, the maintenance history of the carabiners is in question. The carabiners showed signs of excessive wear and pitting on the gate mechanism, indicating long-term misuse and lack of proper maintenance by the user. It is standard practice for users to inspect their gear for wear and tear. The claim that the carabiners were in "pristine condition" is contradicted by the physical evidence of wear on the gate.

Regarding load distribution, the load was concentrated on the gate due to an improper angle of the anchor point, which is not supported by the product's design specifications. The product is not designed to handle lateral shear forces of this magnitude when the gate is engaged in this manner. We stand by the quality of our product. The SecureLock X1 is a safe and reliable piece of equipment when used as intended. The incident was the result of improper use and maintenance, not a manufacturing defect.

=== DOCUMENT 4: Witness Statement - Sarah Jenkins, Lead Hiker (Consumer Safety Watch) ===

**Statement Date:** 16 October 2023
**Subject:** Personal Account of Incident on 14 October 2023

I am the Lead Hiker for the Alpine Safety Watch. I was leading the training session on the day of the incident. The three of us were rappelling down the 450-meter granite face using a 10.8 mm diameter nylon rope. We had set up our anchors according to strict safety protocols.

The rope was positioned correctly according to standard rappelling techniques, with no contact with the carabiner gate. I watched the entire setup process. We double-checked every clip. There was no pinching. There was no improper angle. The load was evenly distributed across the carabiner spine, as per standard safety protocols.

When the carabiner failed, it happened suddenly. The 32 kN load was just the weight of us and the gear, but the way it failed was violent. Dr. Rossi was right; the gate snapped open, and the fracture line was visible even from a distance. I saw the crack in the gate before it fully separated. It was a tiny, hairline crack that expanded rapidly. This is what happens when metal fatigue sets in.

PeakGear Industries is trying to blame us. They claim the rope was pinched. That is a lie. I was right there. I checked the gate. It was clean. I checked the angle. It was perfect. They are using this incident to deflect from the fact that their product is flawed. We have been documenting these failures for years. Twelve reports in five years. It’s not an accident anymore. It’s a pattern.

The carabiners were inspected and found to be in pristine condition with no signs of wear or damage before the incident. We cleaned them. We checked them. There was no pitting. There was no wear. They are trying to say we didn’t maintain them. We are professionals. We maintain our gear.

This incident happened because the carabiner was weak. It was a manufacturing defect. The gate hinge was compromised. I am not going to let them rewrite history by blaming the user. The rope was fine. The anchor was fine. The gear was the problem.

=== DOCUMENT 5: Email Correspondence - Internal Review, PeakGear Industries ===

**From:** Quality Assurance Department
**To:** Marcus Thorne, Head of Communications
**Date:** 15 October 2023
**Subject:** Re: Valtournenche Incident - Data Review

Marcus,

I’ve pulled the batch data for the SecureLock X1 units involved in the Valtournenche incident. As you know, our internal records show that 0.5% of SecureLock X1 units returned for inspection in 2022 failed due to manufacturing defects. This is a known metric we have been tracking, but it is below the industry average for this class of product.

The post-incident analysis confirmed a static load of 32 kN. This is above the rated load capacity of 25 kN. I have reviewed the video footage from the training session. While the angle of the anchor is debatable, the video does show the rope moving slightly as the hikers descended. It is possible, though not confirmed, that there was some interaction between the rope and the gate mechanism.

We need to be careful with our public statements. We cannot admit to a manufacturing defect without a full independent investigation. The EN 362 compliance and the 10,000 cycle fatigue testing are our strongest points. We should emphasize that the load exceeded the rated capacity and that the angle of application was critical.

The customer support line responded within 4 hours, which is good. We should highlight that in the public response. It shows we are responsive.

I recommend we stick to the line that the user applied excessive lateral force and that the maintenance history suggests wear. We have the wear data from the returned unit. The pitting on the gate is consistent with long-term use.

Let’s wait for the final materials report before we commit to any specific technical details about the fracture mode.

Regards,
QA Department
